questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT a valid identity?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- XOR is associative [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.
- Take x = 1, y = 1, z = 0: [latex](x+y)\oplus z=1\oplus0=1[/latex] but [latex]x\oplus(y+z)=1\oplus1=0[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not valid.
- If xy = 0, x and y are never both 1, so XOR equals OR [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.
- [latex]xy+x'y'[/latex] is XNOR; its complement is XOR [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.

Answer: [latex](x+y)\oplus z=x\oplus(y+z)[/latex]

questions.text: If L is a regular language over [latex]\Sigma =\{a,b\}[/latex], which one of the following languages is NOT regular ?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L\cdot L^R[/latex]: regular languages are closed under reversal and concatenation [latex]\text{---}[/latex] regular.
- Prefix(L), Suffix(L): closed operations on regular languages [latex]\text{---}[/latex] regular.
- [latex]\{ww^R\mid w\in L\}[/latex]: take [latex]L=\Sigma^*[/latex]; this gives even-length palindromes, which are not regular.

Answer: [latex]\{ww^R\mid w\in L\}[/latex]

questions.text: Consider Z = X - Y where X, Y and Z are all in sign-magnitude form. X and Y are each represented in n bits. To avoid overflow, the representation of Z would require a minimum of:
questions.solution:
In sign-magnitude, n bits give 1 sign bit and n [latex]-[/latex] 1 magnitude bits. X [latex]-[/latex] Y can be as large as (max magnitude) + (max magnitude), e.g. (+max) [latex]-[/latex] ([latex]-[/latex]max), which needs one more magnitude bit.

So Z needs n + 1 bits.

Answer: n+1 bits

questions.text:
Let X be a square matrix. Consider the following two statements on X.

I. X is invertible
II. Determinant of X is non-zero

Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.solution:
A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero ([latex]X^{-1}=\frac{adj(X)}{\det X}[/latex]). So I and II imply each other.

Answer: I and II are equivalent statements

questions.text:
Let G be an arbitrary group. Consider the following relations on G:

R1: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_1b[/latex] if and only if [latex]\exists g \in G[/latex] such that [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex]
R2: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_2b[/latex] if and only if [latex]a=b^{-1}[/latex]

Which of the above is/are equivalence relation/relations?
questions.solution:
R1 (conjugacy):
- Reflexive: [latex]a=e^{-1}ae[/latex]
- Symmetric: if [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex] then [latex]b=gag^{-1}[/latex]
- Transitive: [latex]a=g^{-1}bg,\ b=h^{-1}ch\Rightarrow a=(hg)^{-1}c(hg)[/latex]
So R1 is an equivalence relation.

R2: aR2a would need [latex]a=a^{-1}[/latex], which fails in general (e.g. 1 in [latex]\mathbb{Z}_3[/latex]). Not reflexive.

Answer: R1 only
